read.sections.0.heading.source: Your feed is chosen for you
read.sections.0.heading.back: Your feed is chosen for you

read.sections.0.text.source: People post far more than anyone could see, so many apps use an algorithm to choose what goes in your feed. An algorithm is a set of steps a computer follows. It learns from what you watched, liked or skipped before. Then it guesses what you will want to see. Apps aim for different things. Some count how long you watch, and some also ask people if they were happy with what they saw. A feed can be very useful. It can help you discover a skill, a song or local news you would never have found. In the made-up town of Maplebrook, Lena liked posts about books, and her feed found her a free video lesson on writing stories. Ravi watched many football videos, so his feed showed him mostly posts about the new sports field.
read.sections.0.text.back: People post more than anyone could ever watch, so many apps use an algorithm to choose what goes in your feed. An algorithm is a set of steps a computer follows. It learns from what you have watched, liked or skipped, then guesses what you will want to see. Each app has different goals: some count how long you watch, and some also ask users whether they are happy with what they see. Feeds can be very useful. They help you discover skills, music or local news you would never find on your own. In a fictional town called Maplebrook, Lena liked posts about books, and her feed found a free video lesson on writing short stories. Ravi watched lots of football videos, so his feed showed mostly posts about the new sports ground.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Feeds and what a town knows
read.sections.1.heading.back: Feeds and what people in a town know

read.sections.1.text.source: Each feed is chosen for one person. So two neighbours can see very different posts about the same town, as Ravi and Lena did before Maplebrook's vote. This matters for public life. To take part in an election, people need some shared, correct facts, such as the day of the vote. A rumour can spread fast. In 2018, researchers at MIT in the United States published a study of about 126,000 news stories shared on Twitter from 2006 to 2017. False stories spread further and faster than true ones. People did most of the sharing, not robot accounts. The study looked at what people shared on one site, so it did not show that feeds or AI caused the spread.
read.sections.1.text.back: Each feed is chosen for one person, so two neighbours may see very different posts about the same town, as Ravi and Lena did before Maplebrook's vote. This matters for public life. To take part in an election, people need some correct facts in common, such as the voting day. Rumours can spread fast. In 2018 researchers at MIT in the United States published a study of about 126,000 news stories people shared on Twitter from 2006 to 2017. Untrue stories spread further and faster than true ones. People did most of the sharing, not robot accounts. This study looked at what people shared on one website, so it does not show that feeds or AI caused the spread.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Each feed is chosen for one person. So two neighbours can see different posts about the same town. Ravi and Lena did before the vote. In an election, people need the same true facts. One is the day of the vote. A rumour can spread fast. In 2018, MIT researchers in the US studied news stories on Twitter. The stories were from 2006 to 2017. False stories spread faster than true ones. People shared them, not only robots. The study looked at what people shared on one site. It did not show that feeds or AI caused this.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Each feed is chosen for one person, so two neighbours may see different posts about the same town. Before the vote Ravi and Lena were like that. In an election people need to know the same correct facts, such as the voting day. Rumours can spread fast. In 2018 researchers at MIT in the United States studied many news stories on Twitter. These stories came from 2006 to 2017. Untrue stories spread faster than true ones. People did the sharing, not just robots. The study looked at what people shared on one website. The study did not show that feeds or AI were the cause.

read.sections.2.heading.source: What the evidence says, and what helps
read.sections.2.heading.back: What the evidence says, and what helps

read.sections.2.text.source: Some people worry that feeds put each of us in a filter bubble, where we only see one side. But in 2022, a review of many studies by the Reuters Institute at the University of Oxford found that real filter bubbles are less common than many people think. People's own choices about what to follow also matter. A European Union law, in full use since 2024, says that very large apps must explain how their feeds choose posts. They must also offer a feed that isn't based on what they know about you. Apps change often, so a study from a few years ago may not describe them today. You can help as well: follow different sources, share the official notice and check before you share.
read.sections.2.text.back: Some people worry that feeds will trap each of us in a filter bubble, where we see only one side. But in 2022 the Reuters Institute at Oxford University reviewed many studies and found that real filter bubbles are less common than many people think. People's own choices about what to follow matter too. A European Union law fully in use since 2024 says very large apps must explain how their feeds choose posts, and must offer a feed that is not based on what the app knows about you. Apps change often, so research from a few years ago may not describe today's apps. You can help too: follow a variety of sources, share official notices and check before sharing.

watch.summary.source: This short news video for young people explains social media algorithms. An algorithm is a set of instructions that tells a computer program what to do. On many apps, the algorithm decides which posts you see and in what order. It also decides which posts you don't see. So when you scroll, you might think you are seeing everything. In fact, someone built a system that chooses for you. How does it choose? It tries to show you posts that will keep you interested, so you keep scrolling. Experts in the video say this isn't always a good thing. Your feed is carefully chosen. It is not a full view of the world. Knowing how your feed is chosen can help you think about what you see.
watch.summary.back: This short news video for young people explains social media algorithms. An algorithm is a set of instructions that tells a computer program what to do. In many apps an algorithm decides which posts you see and in what order. It also decides which posts you will not see. So when you scroll you might think you are seeing everything, but really people built a system that chooses for you. How does the system choose? It tries to show posts that keep you interested so you keep scrolling. The experts in the video say this is not always good. Your feed is chosen on purpose, not a picture of the whole world. Knowing how your feed is chosen helps you think about what you see.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Elections and politics can be painful or dangerous topics for some learners. Keep the discussion on made-up Maplebrook. Never ask learners about elections, politics or votes in any country they have lived in, or how anyone in their family votes, and don't let a debate about real candidates or parties start; steer back to how feeds and rumours work.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: Elections and politics may be painful or dangerous topics for some learners. Talk only about the fictional town of Maplebrook. Do not ask learners about elections, politics or voting in any country they have lived in, or how family members voted, and do not let debate start about real candidates or parties. Bring it back to how feeds and rumours work.

educatorNotes.0.source: The research in section 2 is Vosoughi, Roy and Aral (Science, March 2018; MIT News, 8 March 2018, re-read 8 November 2026): about 126,000 cascades of news stories on Twitter, 2006 to 2017, tweeted over 4.5 million times by about 3 million people, each story judged true or false by six independent fact-checking organisations that agreed over 95% of the time. False news was 70% more likely to be retweeted, and true stories took about six times as long to reach 1,500 people; the gap held with bots removed. Its scope: one platform, those years, and stories that fact-checkers had investigated (contested stories, not all posts). It measured what people retweeted, not how a ranking algorithm chose posts, so it does not show that AI caused the spread; the authors say other platforms need separate study, and that they “cannot claim that novelty causes retweets”.
educatorNotes.0.back: The study in part 2 is Vosoughi, Roy and Aral (Science, March 2018; MIT News, 8 March 2018, reread on 8 November 2026). It studied the spread of about 126,000 news story cascades on Twitter from 2006 to 2017, tweeted more than 4.5 million times by about 3 million people. Each story was judged true or untrue by six independent fact-checking organisations, which agreed more than 95 percent of the time. Untrue news was more than 70 percent more likely to be retweeted, and true stories took about six times longer to reach 1,500 people. The difference remained even after removing bots. Limits of the study: one platform, those years, and stories fact-checkers had investigated (contested stories, not every post). It measured what people retweeted, not how ranking algorithms chose posts, so it does not show AI caused the spread. The authors say other platforms need separate study, and they “cannot claim that novelty causes retweets”.

educatorNotes.1.source: Apps rank posts with different signals and aims; don't reduce them to one motive. For example, YouTube's help page lists watch and search history, subscriptions, likes, dislikes, “not interested” and satisfaction surveys (to understand satisfaction, “not just watch time”). Filter bubbles: the Reuters Institute's 2022 review (Ross Arguedas, Robertson, Fletcher and Nielsen) found echo chambers “much less widespread than is commonly assumed”, “no support for the filter bubble hypothesis”, and an important role for people's own choices (self-selection); research outside the United States is limited. The European rule is the Digital Services Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065): in force 16 November 2022, applying in full from 17 February 2024, and earlier to very large platforms (over 45 million monthly users in the EU), four months after the Commission designated them; they must explain the main settings of their recommender systems, offer one not based on profiling, and assess risks such as the manipulation of elections.
educatorNotes.1.back: Apps rank posts with different signals and goals; do not conclude there is only one motive. For example, YouTube's help page lists watch and search history, channel subscriptions, likes, dislikes, “not interested” and satisfaction surveys (to understand satisfaction, “not just watch time”). On filter bubbles, the Reuters Institute's 2022 review (Ross Arguedas, Robertson, Fletcher and Nielsen) found echo chambers are “much less widespread than is commonly assumed”, “no support for the filter bubble hypothesis”, and that people's own choices (self-selection) play an important role. Research outside the US is still scarce. The European rule is the Digital Services Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2065), in force 16 November 2022, fully applicable from 17 February 2024, and applying to very large platforms (more than 45 million monthly users in the EU) earlier, four months after the European Commission designates them very large platforms. These platforms must explain the main settings of their recommender systems, offer one recommender option not based on user profiling, and assess risks such as election manipulation.
educatorNotes.1.note: "echo chamber" as ห้องเสียงสะท้อน with the English in brackets; "recommender system" as ระบบแนะนำเนื้อหา; "profiling" as การทำโปรไฟล์ผู้ใช้. Quotes from the review translated, not kept in English.

educatorNotes.2.source: Section 3's point that apps change matters: the study's years (2006 to 2017) predate today's feeds, and Twitter is now called X. For discussion or on paper, put Ravi's and Lena's feeds side by side and ask what each friend sees, what each might miss, and how the election office's notice could reach both. There is no sorting task.
educatorNotes.2.back: Part 3's point that apps keep changing matters. The study's years (2006 to 2017) are before today's feeds, and Twitter is now renamed X. For discussion or paper work, put Ravi's and Lena's feeds side by side and ask what each friend sees, what each might miss, and how the election office's notice could reach both. There is no sorting activity.
